reset: Reset puts the original settings.json back.
title: Optimize an eventstream and an eventhouse: throughput, retention, caching and a materialized view
objective_text: Fit an eventstream's throughput and retention to its workload, keep a staging table empty with a zero retention period, cache only the data dashboards read, and serve a latest-value tile from a materialized view.
scenario: A fleet telemetry solution works, but it's slow and costly. The eventstream is set for under 10 MB/s while trucks send up to 40 MB/s. Every table keeps all its data hot forever, including a staging table nobody reads. And a dashboard tile scans all of Telemetry every 30 seconds to find each truck's latest reading.
engine_label: A model of an eventstream's settings and a KQL database's policies, checked on this PC
verifies: Your settings pick the throughput level that covers 40 MB/s, keep events 3 to 7 days, give the staging table a zero retention period with recoverability off behind a transactional update policy, keep Telemetry a year with 30 days hot, leave the database's policies alone, and serve the tile from the materialized part of an arg_max view, as the eventstream settings and Kusto policy pages describe them, checked against a model on this PC.
does_not_verify: That anything gets faster or cheaper. Nothing runs here, and no time or capacity is measured.
That an eventhouse accepts the policies or creates the view. No KQL runs here, and the model uses whole days instead of KQL timespans.
The cost of each throughput level or retention period. The settings page gives the levels' rates, not their prices.

expected.description: FleetStream: event throughput Medium, retention 3 to 7 days. RawEvents: SoftDeletePeriod 0 days, Recoverability Disabled, with Telemetry's update policy still transactional. Telemetry: SoftDeletePeriod 365 days, hot cache 30 days. The database's retention and caching stay null. One materialized view LatestByTruck on Telemetry with arg_max by TruckId, and the tile reads materialized_view("LatestByTruck").

validation.fail: FleetStream's settings don't fit the workload.
validation.pass: FleetStream's throughput and retention fit the workload.

rules.why: Low is for under 10 MB/s, Medium for 10 to 100 MB/s and High for over 100 MB/s. The trucks peak at 40 MB/s.
The default is one day, and events are removed when the retention period ends. A paused destination can only catch up on events the eventstream still holds.

validation.fail: A table keeps data longer than it's needed, or for less time than it's needed.
validation.pass: RawEvents keeps nothing, and Telemetry keeps a year.

rules.why: With a soft-delete period of 0, ingested data isn't committed to the source table, and a transactional update policy still moves it into the target. Nothing reads RawEvents.
With a soft-delete period of 0, Recoverability can only be Disabled.
The zero retention setup relies on a transactional update policy. Without it, a failed transform would lose the batch.

SoftDeletePeriod is how long data is kept available to query. In Kusto, with no policy set, the default is 1,000 years. In Fabric, a KQL database keeps data for 3,650 days by default. Either way, continuously ingested data keeps growing.
A database policy applies to every table that doesn't override it, including the other team's. A soft-delete period of 0 isn't allowed at database level anyway.

validation.fail: Telemetry's hot cache doesn't fit how it's queried.
validation.pass: Telemetry keeps the last 30 days hot.

rules.why: Hot data sits on local SSD and is faster to query. Older data stays queryable from slower, cheaper storage. The dashboards read 30 days, and the analysts accept slower answers for the rest.
Leave the database's caching policy to the other team. A table policy overrides it.

validation.fail: The Latest position tile still aggregates more than it needs to.
validation.pass: The tile reads the materialized part of a latest-reading view.

rules.why: A materialized view keeps an aggregation's result up to date, and querying it commonly performs better than running the aggregation on the source table.
materialized_view() reads only the materialized part. It can be a little behind, but it always performs better than the whole view, which suits telemetry dashboards.

hints: What's the eventstream's default retention, and how long can a weekend outage last?
Who reads RawEvents? What does a soft-delete period of 0 do on a table?
Retention decides what can be queried. Caching decides what's fast. Which needs a year and which needs 30 days?
Why must the policies go on the tables and not on the database?
Which aggregation function returns each truck's latest row, and how does a query read only a view's materialized part?
explanation: Each setting fits one part of the workload. Event throughput sets the level for incoming and outgoing events. Low is under 10 MB/s, so 40 MB/s needs Medium, which covers 10 to 100 MB/s. If you change it on a running stream with a custom endpoint, the partition count goes up and the sending client might need an update. The eventstream keeps events one day by default, up to 90, and a paused destination can only catch up on events still held, so 3 to 7 days covers a weekend. In the eventhouse, retention and caching are separate. Retention sets how long data stays queryable, and caching sets what stays hot on fast local SSD. In Kusto, with no policy set, data is kept for 1,000 years and all of it is hot. In Fabric, a KQL database keeps data for 3,650 days and caches it for 3,650 days by default. This model starts with no policy set. Telemetry needs a year queryable but only 30 days hot, because older queries can be slower. RawEvents only feeds a transactional update policy, so a soft-delete period of 0 keeps it empty, and that setting requires recoverability off. Both policies go on the tables, because a database policy would change the other team's tables, and 0 isn't allowed at database level. Last, the tile runs an arg_max over all of Telemetry every 30 seconds. A materialized view keeps that result up to date, and materialized_view() reads only its materialized part. That's faster still, at the cost of being a little behind, which is fine for this tile.
review_notes: Checked on Learn 2026-11-23. configure-settings: retention defaults to one day, events are removed when it expires, maximum 90 days. Event throughput levels are Low under 10 MB/s, Medium 10 to 100 MB/s and High over 100 MB/s. Changing throughput may need nodes that support pause and resume deactivated, and custom endpoint clients may need an update because the partition count increases. Lab-tested upper limits for Eventhouse (Event processing before ingestion) are about 20, 100 and 200 MB/s for Low, Medium and High.

retention-policy: SoftDeletePeriod is how long data is guaranteed to be kept available to query, default 1,000 years. A table policy overrides the database policy. A soft-delete period of 0 is allowed on a table but not on a database. Then ingested data isn't committed to the source table, Recoverability can only be Disabled, and the setup is meant for a transactional update policy that moves the data to another table. Setting a retention policy limits cost when ingesting continuously.

Checked on Learn 2026-11-28. retention-policy: when a database or table is created it has no retention policy, and .show gives null. SoftDeletePeriod defaults to 1,000 years. cache-policy: by default the effective policy is null, which means all data is hot, and a null table policy inherits the database's. data-policies (Fabric, updated 2026-03-22): the default retention policy is 3,650 days, with a maximum of 36,500, and data is cached for 3,650 days by default. So 36,500 days is Fabric's maximum, not its default. No rule depends on any of these defaults. The rules rest on the scenario's needs.

cache-policy: hot data is on local SSD and faster, cold data is in cheaper, slower storage. A null policy means all data is hot, and a table policy overrides the database. Caching is independent of retention, and the page's example queries the full retained period while only part is hot.

materialized-view-overview: a view exposes an aggregation over a source table, is always fresh, and querying it commonly performs better than the source. materialized_view() queries only the materialized part, isn't guaranteed to be most up to date, always performs better, and suits telemetry dashboards. An arg_max view works best when the records updated are a small subset of the source.

Whether High costs more than Medium isn't on the settings page, so the rule rests on the stated level ranges, not on price. The 3 to 7 day range and the 365 and 30 day values come from the scenario's needs, not from Learn.
